story_text.value:
What this is: Each day there's one target species, and you classify it level by level (from more general to more specific categories), with 10 seconds per choice. Faster answers score more, and there are daily and monthly leaderboards.

Why: I wanted to try out agentic coding (a bit late to the party I know). A friend gifted me a week of Claude, and this is what I got in 3 afternoons of full vibe-coding. I've had the idea for this game for a while (I'm a philosopher of biology), and this was a good toy project for it. I'd never vibe-code like this in a serious project, but wanted to see how far I could get / how good frontier models were, and I'm honestly impressed. I have mixed feelings about the whole experience, but I could have never done this so fast without it.

Stack: It's made with Svelte 5 and CF workers & D1. I've worked with both in the past and knew it's good for a little (free to host) side project like this.

Feedback welcome, especially on whether the 10 seconds feels right (I wanted to avoid people googling the categories while playing).

story_text.value:
McKinley is a Mac app for making SF Symbols. It costs $60 (one off purchase).

SF Symbols are Apple's vector symbol format. The OS ships with thousands of them, but you can make your own for your own apps.

The recommended way to make SF Symbols is to export a template from Apple's helper app, edit it in a vector editor, then re-import it and tag all the SF Symbol specific metadata.

This process is usually a pain in the ass. SF Symbols support multiple weights -- you draw three, and Apple interpolates between them. This means that each of your weights needs to have the same paths in the same order, with the same number of points. Everything has to be converted to outlines for the interpolation to work, it doesn't render strokes.

McKinley is my attempt to save you from that. It's a vector editor that is built around the constraints of SF Symbols. You can edit your symbol while flicking between the three weights or the four colour modes. It can save SF Symbol files or sync straight to Xcode asset catalogs. You don't have to bounce between a vector editor and a symbols converter, because McKinley is both.

I'm pleased with how live previews work. I wanted to offer a preview with Apple's own renderer. But you can't load an SF Symbol in-memory at runtime. So I figured out the file format for asset catalogs, and create a temporary one and load _that_. (I blogged about how I did it: https://www.amyworrall.com/blog/previewing-sf-symbols-with-a... )

A couple of things I know people will ask:

* It's a native AppKit app (not Electron or anything cross-platform) * Sold directly from my site via Stripe, not Mac App Store. * One-time purchase. License is valid on up to 5 computers, and covers all version 1.x updates. * There's a 14 day free trial, which includes saving/exporting * It is sandboxed, notarised, and all that good stuff * No analytics or network traffic, apart from updates (handled by Sparkle) and license checking (handled by Amore).

Happy to answer any questions or dive into technical details if people want :)

story_text.value:
In 2019, I was teaching science at an international school in Chiang Mai. One day before class, one of my Grade 7 students asked me about flat earth. He had heard the idea from Kyrie Irving and then spent the night on flat earth sites.

We walked through the claims and I explained why those arguments failed. He listened with interest. I was glad he'd come to me. He hadn't made up his mind yet; he was just curious. But this made me wonder if teaching the course content I was teaching was enough.

To be clear: I do think teaching facts is important. For example, when students learn about gravity, physics, and space, they're better prepared to see why flat earth arguments are wrong. The problem is we can't teach facts fast enough to combat the wide variety of misinformation and manipulation kids face on the internet every day.

This is what got me thinking that kids need to learn how to evaluate claims and information across a wide range of topics. While we can't prepare them for every false or misleading claim they might encounter, we can give them tools to assess them.

That eventually led my husband and I to build Critikid, a site for teaching kids and teens. We've been working on it for 3 years now! He does the technical work (design and coding) and I do the educational content creation.

By now, there are 5 interactive courses for ages 5-18 on logical fallacies, media literacy, emotional intelligence, statistical reasoning, and formal logic. There are also worksheets and lesson plans.

I often teach through stories, as stories make abstract critical thinking concepts concrete (and they're fun!)

If you'd like to try it, all of the courses have a free first lesson.

Are there any other topics that you think should be included in kids' critical thinking education that I've missed?

story_text.value:
Zebu is a time tracking and invoicing app for freelancers and small teams. It's €5 per seat per month (billed yearly), flat, with no usage fees. There's a limited free plan for solo use.

I built it after 15 years as a solo freelancer on Harvest. After they were acquired, my renewal exploded from $12/month to ~$180/month, and unclear usage based pricing made it hard to predict how much it would always cost. The BBC even reported customers seeing increases of 1,500% - https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/clyq011414eo.

I've been working on a replacement for the past year, and am happy to say my colleagues and I now use it full-time. In many ways it even surpasses the featureset I'd had on Harvest - it's really kind of amazing what kind of custom tooling one can build these days.

I'd especially like feedback on how the migration is working from any services you might come from, any critical integrations that might be useful, and especially what might be missing for team use.

story_text.value:
Thoreau BASIC started as a joke. I wanted a BASIC where I could type something ridiculous like:

  DIM A%(12000000000)
…and have it actually work. Then I kept adding things. The result is Thoreau BASIC, a free x64 BASIC interpreter inspired by GW-BASIC, running both as a normal Windows program and directly on bare-metal UEFI without an operating system.

Version 3.2 has become considerably more ambitious than the little interpreter I originally intended to write. The language still deliberately looks and feels like old Microsoft BASIC. Line numbers, GOTO, GOSUB, PRINT, PSET, LINE, CIRCLE, DRAW, etc. are all there. But underneath that rather innocent-looking surface is now quite a lot of machinery.

Some of the current features:

  native x64 JIT compilation, with automatic fallback to the interpreter
  PARFOR for multithreaded numeric loops
  SSE2 / AVX2 acceleration where available
  64-bit addressing and very large arrays
  native complex, quaternion and other hypercomplex numbers
  arbitrary-resolution 24-bit graphics
  sprites, bitmap operations, polygon filling and mouse input
  TCP/IP networking on Windows and UEFI
  an integrated profiler, debugger, tracing and program-analysis tools
  CREATEEXE to turn a BASIC program into a standalone Windows executable
  CREATEEFI to turn the same program into a directly bootable UEFI application
The sound system has also grown rather out of proportion. Thoreau BASIC can now handle up to 32 live instrument channels plus 64 sound effect channels and 256 voices, with real-time pan and brightness control. NOTE and SOUNDKEY can be used more like playable synthesis primitives rather than just old-school BASIC beeps.

3.2 also expands the less glamorous but surprisingly useful parts of the environment. There is better file browsing and selection with GETFILES and SELECTBOX, longer case-preserving paths, recovery/file-flush facilities, and considerably more detailed SYSTEMINFO$ diagnostics. The latter is useful for seeing things such as available CPU capabilities and the execution environment while debugging performance differences between machines.

One thing I've spent a lot of time on recently is making the BASIC programs themselves fast enough that they stop feeling like demonstrations of an interpreter. For example, the current Mandelbrot demo is a real-time interactive fractal explorer. Mouse movement pans the fractal, left-click zooms in and right-click zooms out, while the BASIC program continuously redraws and displays the frame rate.

There are also 3D and procedural demos, sprite programs, networking examples, hypercomplex fractals and games. An important design constraint throughout the project has been that Windows and UEFI should execute essentially the same BASIC language. A program shouldn't suddenly become a different species just because there is no operating system underneath it.

And yes, I am fully aware of the absurdity of combining GOTO 100 with AVX2, multithreading, TCP/IP and quaternion arithmetic. That is increasingly the point. I'm interested in the question: What would BASIC look like if it had never gone out of fashion? Thoreau BASIC 3.2 is my current answer.

I'd be especially interested in feedback from people who remember GW-BASIC/QBasic, compiler/interpreter people, and anyone sufficiently unreasonable to enjoy the idea of booting a modern x64 PC directly into a BASIC interpreter/JIT compiler.

title.value: Show HN: Thoreau BASIC – What if BASIC hadn't gone out of fashion?

story_text.value:
I'm a small indie developer, I've made a mac app called Sidekins

It is a small desktop character that you can design yourself(I call it a Kin/Sidekin) and lives around your screen and peeps from the side when not in use.

It is a very social app, you can add your friends and chat with them using your Kin. It is an AI agent so you can ask in the main chat to delivery some message to your friend and it creates the message you want and animation using your Kin and goes to your friends desktop and speaks/act out your message.

You can also ask it to help you "guide" through your mac, or any app, it moves and points around telling you how things work. There is also a "do" mode, this actually does things for you on your mac, like play this song on Spotify or add an iPhone 16 to my amazon cart.

you can see the demos here on the website on what and how it does things : www.sidekins.com

Currently, it works on Mac with apple silicon, and has 300 free messages.

Try it out, and connect with me on the app: @18kushaljain

story_text.value:
(Edit: original URL was https://againstallodds.games/, but we've switched it to https://againstallodds.games/blog/2026/10/03/our-risc-v-emul... in response to user requests for explanation.)

We're a tiny indie studio, all with a background in the demoscene and for about 3 years now we're developing a space planet terraforming game called SEEDS - Echoes Beneath the Sands.

Our protagonist Naxiah is stranded on a small, desolated planet. You're working for an intergalactic distributor of seeds and terraforming equipment, to kickstart new planets in far away galaxies. You must deliver seeds and utilities to an unchartered region, but on your way, you crash on a small planet. Luckily, you have some equipment with you in the ship, so you're able to spawn a base and survive. But for how long? And is the planet really deserted..? :) Well, of course not, there are aliens and other space creatures. And of course, there's ROBO RB-23, which accompanies your adventure.

The game is written in Object Pascal and uses our own game engine PasVulkan, our own physics engine, as well as our own RISC-V 64-bit emulator PasRISCV. We love to build stuff, a lot of these things are FOSS.

The emulator is quite complete (even with RVV, but that's way too slow emulated to be useful) and runs a stock kernel (6.18.3 as of today). We're using Alpine Linux for our base distribution. All our in-game programs to interact with the planet are native RISC-V Linux programs.

We also have our own (free and open source) scripting language POCA (class and prototyped based, JS/Lua inspired, which makes it quite easy for us to script things like HUD, animal behaviour, our story flow graph, etc.

We have most of the wiring ready for players to be able to program and reshape and populate the whole planet in automation, although it's not our primary concept for the game (building stuff by hand, making the planet beautiful is also fun). As it's a normal Linux system, you'll be able to use Ruby, Python, or even Rust, C, C++, and Go to change and automate your world.

We're also thinking of making a bunch of small games which you can play inside the game, in the base on a computer, on an arcade machine, or in the spaceship. And of course, it also runs DOOM. We already prototyped a small 2D space shooter and a small arcade game, both playable within the game. We also feature a table with hologram games to be played, e.g. chess and a certain block game. We also plan to make this hologram game engine available from the computer, which means, you'll even be able to program own hologram style games.

We generally want to make the in-game computer more hackable in future, so that people can create and share their own little games.

Currently, it's only a sandbox game (with beginnings of automation), to build stuff with our pre-made items. You can also assemble these to other, ready-made and shareable bigger items. This is the foundation for us to further develop survival and complete our story mode.

Our game is still under active development, and we finally got our Steam page ready. We have tons of other things planned, but right now, it's more about polishing and quality for the Early Access.

You can watch some videos and screenshots on our website. And we'd love to read your thoughts about his. It has been quite a ride, so far..

story_text.value:
I built NeuroDual, a brain-training game app with five guided paths: visual memory, auditory memory, timing, hand laterality, and spatial reasoning.

Each path starts with a baseline test, followed by a series of guided exercises. Every eight sessions, you take the test again. This cycle continues as you work toward your goals. You can also explore the exercises freely in the Lab.

The collection includes classic Dual N-Back and several reworkings of it, alongside Operation Span, Stroop, object tracking, and puzzles such as Gridlock (a Rush Hour-style sliding puzzle), Untangle, Sokoban, and Lights Out. There are over 30 configurable exercises.

The scores track performance on these tasks; they aren't IQ estimates or a promise of broader cognitive gains.

You can try it in your browser without an account. It is also available on Android. The full app has a 90-minute free trial, then a one-time €6.99 unlock, with no subscription.

Short videos of the games and N-Back variants: https://www.youtube.com/@NeuroDual/shorts

A more technical walkthrough of N-Back: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xic1VWHmNdE

story_text.value:
This project doesn't solve a burning problem for me, but it's more of a curiosity-driven experiment asking one question: with LLMs and fuzzing, how close can I get to a 100% Excel-compatible spreadsheet engine?

After working on this for a couple of months, it seems to be pretty close now (and in some cases, more accurate than Excel). Recent fuzzing runs have been unable to find discrepancies with Excel, but I think that there is still a long tail of cases out there. tl;dr: tilion is building the world's fastest and stealthiest browser infra for agents, so you can run millions of web agents successfully. today, we're releasing v3 of our engine, fortress, free for devs.

https://github.com/tiliondev/fortress

launch vid:

i am arham, cto of tilion (ycf26), and we (arman, abdul, and fardin) are building browser infra for agents.

before tilion, we were running thousands of web agents to collect multimodal school board data across the web. our agents kept getting blocked: cloudflare, akamai, captchas, and 200s that were actually empty pages. so we dug into chromium itself.

what we found:

- sites fingerprint the browser in about 40 places (gpu, canvas, fonts, timezone, and so on). a real machine is consistent in all of them, unlike a program-driven browser.

- plugins like puppeteer-stealth and undetected-chromedriver mostly patch from javascript, and the patch itself is detectable. (the irony)

- residential proxies fix the ip, but they're expensive. and if the fingerprint is wrong, you get blocked anyway. so we built and open sourced fortress.

our latest build has 81+ patches in c++. if an anti-bot system checks the browser, it all green-lights on its end.

in practice that means:

- you have higher success rates against blocks. - your proxy bill drops by half. - your agents can do more shit.

theres also a cli and mcp so you can get setup fast. we have windows, mac, and linux native builds. we'll also be launching our cloud browsers, for which we are running millions of agents every day for our pilots request an invite here. [https://tilion.com]

much love. arham

story_text.value:
I love keybr, but it only sees the ten minutes a day I spend on keybr, not the ten hours I spend typing elsewhere. Can’t improve what you don’t measure.

(A)I made Fumble is a macOS menu-bar app that watches you type (all day, all local), works out which keys/key pairs are costing you time and gives you lessons built around them.

One thing that surprised me: my slowest key is B, but the one costing me the most time is G. It's less than half as slow, but I press it three times as often. And 7 of my 10 worst key pairs start with space. I need to get better at starting words.

Some design decisions HN might want to argue with:

- I rank weak keys by time lost, not how slow they are. Time lost is how far a key is over your baseline, times how often you press it. A key 40ms slow that you hit 2k times costs more than one 220ms slow that you hit 50 times. The goal isn't to practice the slowest keys, it's to raise your WPM.

- Your baseline is the median of your own per-key p95s, not the p95 of every keystroke pooled together. Pooling lets a common slow key drag the baseline up and hide itself, and those are the keys that slow down the whole show.

- Slow finger vs thinking: pause adapts to each key pair based on your own median for that pair. There's no flat cutoff.

- The WPM figure shows you what it left out: keystrokes injected by software (text expanders, Keyboard Maestro, osascript), autorepeat, idle time and practice sessions. Every exclusion can be seen in the dropdown.

Privacy: it records physical keycodes and timings not characters. What goes to disk is counters and latency histograms, with no keystroke sequence. Also records nothing while a password field has focus. There's no network code/account/telemetry. PRIVACY.md lists the remaining risk (adjacent-pair frequencies) and gives commands to verify all of this yourself.

It can't be on the Mac App Store, because it needs Input Monitoring and the store requires sandboxing. The download is signed and notarized, so it opens like any normal Mac app.

Free and open source, written in Swift for macOS 14+.

Download: https://fumble.alexmcconnell.ie Source: https://github.com/alexiscodingbits/Fumble

Warning: early days. Not everything has been tested in the wild yet.

The thing I'd most like ideas on is word choice for the weak-spot drills. Right now it takes my top 5 weak keys and top 5 weak pairs and leans towards words that contain them. That treats every weak spot as equal, and it picks words one at a time. What I actually want is the set of 30 words that wins back the most time overall, weighted by how much each weak spot is costing me. It feels like a set-cover problem, and I'm sure there's a smarter way to do it than mine. If you've worked on anything like this, I'd love to hear how you'd approach it.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Justin.

Breadcrumb records everything you do on your Mac (screen + meetings + AI transcripts + what you and your AI decided) and turns it into memory your AI can search. It's local and encrypted.

You can also teach it rules by talking to it and it makes sure the right rules turn up in the right context. Works with Claude Code / Codex / Cursor / opencode.

All of this is exposed to your AI as 30+ MCP tools (here's the definitions): https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/mcp

I started it in June because I wanted to understand what was going on with my AI dev work. Then it just kept growing as I jammed on it 10 hours a day for 3 months.

I started by recording every screen so I could jump back to a moment and see what I'd been doing with the AI. Then I added MCP so the AI could search it. Then time tracking. Then meetings with transcripts and timestamped screenshots.

After that I started feeding the data back in. At first it was just a few relevant memories in the prompt. Then I started adding rules and rules modules.

Then I started recording the AI transcripts and all the other stuff the AI did (subagents, tools etc). I wanted a complete record so I could go back and see what the AI did and why.

I found the more data the AI had the more useful it became. One example. I got off a zoom call with the team at the day job and said:

"Review the meeting I just had, find all the bugs we discussed, and create JIRA tickets with screenshots."

It read the transcript. Found every bug we mentioned, pulled the screens from the screen timeline, spun up my local server, diagnosed each bug, reviewed the code, created 14 tickets in JIRA with diagnosis and likely fixes, attached 12 screenshots as evidence, and created a nice Slack message to send to my colleagues.

I never built a workflow for any of that. Claude had the meeting record, Breadcrumb tools, and rules I'd accumulated. It basically chained the steps together itself.

My favorite thing about the system is observability of my own work as an AI developer. I can trace a bug all the way back to the first thing I said (or the first thing the AI did) that caused it. Then I can add a rule so it doesn't happen again.

Anyway, my working system is simply Claude Desktop + Breadcrumb + Markdown. I find I don't need anything else.

It's local software for one person. Local models for transcription and diarization. Data encrypted with SQLCipher and a passphrase. You can exclude any apps, websites, words and phrases.

Breadcrumb itself only makes one network call which is a daily update check. (but of course your AI will use it and that is local or cloud depending on what you use).

It runs cool about 12% of one core on average (M series mac has 8+). You can set it to just save OCR text or to save screenshots. If just OCR it's about 12mb day (a lot of telemetry, indexing etc). If you record screenshots on meetings it's about 120mb/hour (1 every 2 secs). It can also record screenshots of everything that's heavy at about 160mb/day. It does local classification/naming with ollama with Gemma 3 4B (2.5 GB).

It's 100% free. There's no account you can just download and start using it. I'll monetize it via E2EE cloud sync and team sync. It's open beta. Just one developer working on it. Requires 16GB+ M Series Mac.

Thanks for reading!

https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb (homepage)

https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/download (direct download)

https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/mcp (mcp definition)

story_text.value:
I've shared a few deadlift demos in the past. This new demo includes some new models, accessed through the VLM Run Gateway:

- SAM 3.1 to segment the barbell weight plate

- ViTPose+ Large to measure the hip hinge angle, which serves as a backup for segmenting the reps. The pose data can definitely be used more later.

- Gemma 4 26B through the Gateway's TypeSafe-compatible API to output the probability of the back being rounded or not. The predictions line up well with how I intentionally performed each rep.

Of course, there are many caveats to what is good form, as it depends on the individual. All said, this has the pieces in place to quickly make adjustments to fit the individual better.

In short, a tool like this gives people data to assess their form and improve over time.

Let me know what you think!

Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=917J5oOvcBM

story_text.value:
https://github.com/freakynit/autobox

First of all: this is NOT for folks who are already using a sandbox. The guarantees provided by Autobox are weaker. This is rather for folks who "hesitate" to use sandboxes.

Autobox is built around two observations I kept making over past one year of seeing sandbox launches and their real-world usage:

1. There are many sandboxing options now, and they work well. But leaving a handful few, almost nobody uses them. The blocker isn't the technology, it's the setup friction — however small it looks on paper, it's enough that people skip it entirely.

2. LLMs mostly don't write harmful code or take destructive steps. They're not adversarial by default.

Autobox bets on the second observation to remove the first. Instead of asking you to configure a sandbox, it's just there: every tool call carries its own permissions, and anything you don't explicitly allow is denied.

Is it perfect? No - seatbelt filesystem rules are best-effort, and the strong isolation is the V8 path.

Is it better than using no sandbox at all? Definitely yes.

This is also for M-series Macs only.

---

Oh, and the best part: "copy_then_sync":

Using APPFS `clonefile`, Autobox can hand your agent a full, "writable" copy of a repo instantly (1-2 ms). The agent gets something it can freely "destroy", but, your actual working tree is untouched. Your agent can then verify things, and of all looks okay, in one command sync the changes back to host within milliseconds.

story_text.value:
Almost a year has passed since Desbordante’s last release, and now we’re rolling out a new one — 2.5.0.

Desbordante is an open-source, high-performance data profiler that finds and validates complex patterns in data using a bunch of advanced algorithms.

Unlike the black-box ML approaches that dominate today, Desbordante takes a symbolic, explainable approach to data analysis, producing explicit rules or rule-shaped artifacts that are verifiable, such as data dependencies, association rules, or other patterns. It’s a different way to analyze data, and it works well alongside black-box models. Unlike free-form model output, these patterns have precise semantics and can be validated algorithmically against the data. And, importantly, no hallucinations or misclassification.

This release adds 9 new patterns, including support for another dataset type: sequences in data. That brings the total to 4. We also picked up Python 3.15, which just came out. On top of the new patterns, there was a lot of infrastructure work too — mostly invisible to users, but important.

Full changelog: https://github.com/Desbordante/desbordante-core/releases/tag...
